Treatment with varicella-zoster immune globulin can reduce the severity of neonatal varicella and can prevent neonatal acquisition of the disease. Treatment prevents serious or fatal neonatal complications. Acyclovir therapy (Choice B) is indicated once neonatal varicella symptoms clinically manifest and is not part of routine postexposure prophylaxis. Immune globulin therapy (Choice C) is an acceptable alternative to varicella-zoster immune globulin but only if the latter, preferred treatment is unavailable. Interferon therapy (Choice D) is useful for the treatment of hepatitis Band C. It is not commonly used to treat varicella and has potentially serious side effects including neutropenia and flu-like illness. Educational Objective: Perinatal vertical transmission of varicella zoster virus can lead to neonatal varicella, which presents with fever, generalized vesicular rash, and in severe cases, with organ involvement, including meningoencephalitis, pneumonia, and hepatitis. Exposed newborns should be given postexposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immune globulin.

questionStem: A widowed 37-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 3, whose youngest child is 10 years old, has had increasingly heavy but regular menstrual periods for the past 3 years . Her last menses occurred 2½ weeks ago. She reports a 2-day history of labor-like pains accompanied by a small amount of vaginal bleeding . Speculum examination shows that the cervix is moderately effaced and 2 cm dilated , with some beefy red tissue at the os. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Leiomyomata uteri, also known as uterine fibroids, are benign neoplasms of uterine myometrium and the most common tumor in women. They commonly present with vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, and miscarriage or infertility, and they are more common in African American patients. Physical examination will show an enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus. In the case of pedunculated intracavitary uterine fibroids, or fibroids that grow on a stalk, the pressure on the internal cervical os can cause dilation and effacement of the cervix with protrusion of the fibroid, as seen in this patient. Laboratory studies may show iron deficiency anemia if uterine bleeding is significant. Fibroids are typically well-visualized on pelvic ultrasonography. They are estrogen responsive, causing increases in size with pregnancy and decreases in size with menopause. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral contraceptives, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists, and surgical options such as myomectomy or hysterectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Carcinoma of the cervix (Choice A) presents with vaginal bleeding, classically postcoital, but can be asymptomatic. It is associated with human papillomavirus high risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Physical examination will show an exophytic lesion of the cervix, not a mass protruding through the cervical os as seen in this patient. Risk factors include smoking, multiple sexual partners, and an immunocompromised state. Carcinoma of the endometrium (Choice B) commonly presents as postmenopausal bleeding, with a thickened endometrium on pelvic ultrasonography. Risk factors include prolonged exposure to estrogen, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, obesity, and diabetes. It does not present with a mass at the cervical os, and pelvic pain is an uncommon symptom. Incomplete abortion (Choice C) occurs when a fetus expires and there is partial expulsion of fetal tissue through an open cervical os. It is typically associated with pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. As not all products are expelled, treatment consists of expectant management, uterine aspiration, or dilation and curettage. As this patient's last menses was two and a half weeks ago, it is unlikely her symptoms are caused by a pregnancy. Sarcoma of the uterus (Choice E) is a rare malignant tumor of the myometrium. It presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, and bloating. It is unlikely to present with dilation and effacement of the cervix, as seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Leiomyomata uteri, or uterine fibroids, are estrogen-sensitive, benign neoplasms of the uterine myometrium that present with vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, and miscarriage or infertility. The uterus will be large and irregularly shaped on physical examination, with pedunculated intracavitary masses causing possible dilation and effacement of the cervix. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral contraceptives, gonadotropin-release hormone agonists, and surgical options (eg, myomectomy or hysterectomy).

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 7 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. She has no history of serious illness , and pregnancy has been uncomplicated . She began taking a prenatal vitamin 3 weeks ago. Physical examination, including pelvic examination , shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Measurement of serum folic acid concentration
choices.E: Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration

correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Hematocrit Mean corpuscular volume Serum Ferritin Iron 10.1g/dl 30% 72 µm3 110 ng/ml 130 µg/dl Hemoglobin electrophoresis would be the next step in evaluation for this patient at an early gestational age who has microcytic anemia with normal iron studies. While a mild decrease in hemoglobin is common in pregnancy secondary to a physiologic increase in plasma volume, a hemoglobin concentration less than 10.5 g/dl is considered abnormal and should be evaluated. Microcytosis, defined as a mean corpuscular volume less than 80 µm3, can be caused by iron deficiency, sideroblastic anemia, anemia of chronic disease, and thalassemia, among other rare causes. Iron deficiency is unlikely in this patient because she has a normal ferritin and serum iron concentration. Similarly, anemia of chronic disease presents with normal to high ferritin concentration and low iron concentration in chronic inflammation. Sideroblastic anemia is much less common than other causes of microcytosis, and is often related to lead poisoning, Vitamin B6 deficiency, isoniazid, and alcoholism. It would typically present with increased iron concentration, basophilic stippling on peripheral smear, and ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain. Hemoglobin electrophoresis can be used to assess for thalassemia, distinguishing between a-thalassemia (major or trait), and 13- thalassemia (major or minor), and it would be the next most reasonable step in testing. Discovery of one of these conditions may have implications for both the mother and the fetus.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. a-Globin DNA testing (Choice A) is reserved for patients with suspected a-thalassemia trait. These patients often have a normal hemoglobin electrophoresis. This would not be the most appropriate first step but could be considered as confirmatory testing of suspected a-thalassemia trait after hemoglobin electrophoresis. Hemoglobin solubility testing (Choice C) is used to identify the presence of HbS, which is the abnormal 13-globin protein found in sickle cell disease and sickle cell trait. It only identifies the presence of HbS and would not be able to provide information on the presence or absence of other forms of hemoglobin that may point toward an alternative diagnosis. Measurement of serum folic acid concentration (Choice D) would be performed to assess for folic acid deficiency in patients with macrocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia. Patients who are suspected of having folate deficiency are treated presumptively. Additionally, all gravid patients should be taking folate supplements. Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration (Choice E) would be reasonable if the patient had macrocytic anemia. Vitamin B 12 deficiency can also result in neurologic dysfunction such as subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. It is most often seen in patients with prior gastric bypass, Crohn disease, and pernicious anemia. Educational Objective: Decreased hemoglobin concentrations are common in pregnancy because of a physiologic increase in plasma volume, but hemoglobin concentrations below 10.5 g/dl with microcytosis should be further evaluated. Iron studies are often obtained first to rule out iron deficiency, but if normal, should be followed by hemoglobin electrophoresis for the assessment of thalassemia.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has tested positive for the factor V Leiden mutation . Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated , and she delivered at term by cesarean section for breech presentation . She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and has continued to smoke during pregnancy . She does not drink alcohol. She maintains a vegan diet, and she owns and manages a vegetarian restaurant. She lives at home with her partner and son. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Ultrasonography shows a fetus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation with normal amniotic fluid volume . The placenta is anterior, and the distal portion covers the internal cervical os. Which of the following is the greatest predisposing factor for this patient's findings on ultrasonography?
correctExplanation: Placenta previa refers to the abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. Placenta previa is usually detected, as in this patient, on routine prenatal ultrasonography. Its most common presenting symptom is third trimester painless vaginal bleeding. Risk factors for placenta previa include causes of uterine scarring, such as multiparity, previous cesarean delivery, and prior dilation and curettage. The condition often self-resolves as gestation progresses, and the placenta migrates away from the os. If placenta previa persists into the third trimester and to the time of labor, cesarean delivery is indicated to prevent significant hemorrhage, maternal/fetal complications, and potential fetal demise.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Maternal age (Choice A) may contribute to the risk of placenta previa, fetal trisomy, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and preeclampsia. This patient's history of previous cesarean delivery is the greatest predisposing risk factor for the development of placenta previa. Nutritional status (Choice B) increases the risk of fetal malformations, including neural tube defects. Maternal nutritional status does not significantly alter the risk of placenta previa. Smoking history (Choice D) increases the risk of placenta previa, but not to as great an extent as a prior cesarean delivery. Thrombophilia (Choice E), such as in antiphospholipid syndrome, is an important cause of placental ischemic injury, fetal hypoxia, and miscarriage. It is not a risk factor for placenta previa. Educational Objective: Placenta previa refers to the abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. Risk factors for placenta previa include causes of uterine scarring, such as multiparity, previous cesarean delivery, and prior dilation and curettage.

questionStem: A 36-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 41 weeks' gestation has had ruptured membranes without contractions for 8 hours. Her first infant weighed 4422 g (9 lb 12 oz) at birth. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated except for gestational diabetes , which was diagnosed at 26 weeks' gestation and has been well controlled with diet. Initial assessment shows a fundal height of 40 cm. On ultrasonography , the estimated fetal weight is 3714 g (8 lb 3 oz). The cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50% effaced . The fetal heart rate is within normal limits. Labor is induced with intravenous oxytocin . Four hours later, her cervix is 4 cm dilated and completely effaced . Continuous epidural anesthesia is administered . Two hours later, the fetal heart rate pattern demonstrates late decelerations with each contraction . The contractions occur every minute , last 45 seconds , and are 75 mm Hg at their peak. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern ?
correctExplanation: Oxytocin is frequently administered to induce or augment labor. It acts by stimulating uterine contraction, which in turn leads to the progressive dilation and effacement of the cervix. It is also used after delivery to induce uterine contraction in the setting of uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage. However, when a patient receives too much oxytocin, hyperstimulation or tachysystole of the uterus can occur in which the uterus contracts too frequently without adequate relaxation time (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes), often with prolongation and intensification of the contraction or lack of return to a resting tone. These contractions can cause compression of the placental blood vessels, leading to uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia. This often presents with late decelerations on the fetal heart tracing, or gradual decreases in the fetal heart rate that begin after the peak uterine contraction. Treatment includes the discontinuation of the administered oxytocin, followed by close monitoring of the fetal heart tracing to assess for resolution of the late decelerations. If the late decelerations persist after the cessation of the oxytocin, there may be an additional cause for the uteroplacental insufficiency, and an urgent cesarean delivery may be indicated for persistent fetal hypoxemia. Another potential complication of uterine tachysystole is uterine rupture.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Epidural anesthesia (Choice A) can cause uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxemia if the epidural results in maternal hypotension. It is unlikely to cause late decelerations in the absence of low maternal blood pressure and does not cause changes in uterine contractions. Fetal macrosomia (Choice B) can present with shoulder dystocia, prolonged labor, or postpartum uterine atony. It is commonly associated with maternal gestational diabetes, which also increases the risk for uteroplacental insufficiency. However, fetal macrosomia does not cause tachysystole. Gestational diabetes (Choice C) increases the risk for uteroplacental insufficiency and associated late decelerations. It can also cause preterm labor, polyhydramnios, and macrosomia. It does not cause tachysystole. Postdates pregnancy (Choice E) can be associated with macrosomia, oligohydramnios, and uteroplacental insufficiency. However, given the change in uterine contraction with the initiation of oxytocin, oxytocin administration is more likely the cause of the late decelerations. Educational Objective: Oxytocin can be used to induce or augment labor, but high doses are associated with tachysystole (greater than five contractions in 10 minutes), prolonged contractions, intense contractions, and delayed or absent return to resting tone. This can cause placental blood vessel compression, uteroplacental insufficiency, fetal hypoxemia, and late decelerations on the fetal heart tracing.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of urinary urgency and frequency and occasional incontinence and a 2-month history of numbness below her waist. She has had to get up at least three times at night to void. She has not had fever, pain with urination , or cloudy urine. She has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis ; symptoms have included double vision 10 years ago and right leg weakness 3 years ago. Sensation to vibration is decreased over both feet. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ at the knees. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Her postvoid residual volume is 45 ml. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's urinary findings?

choices.E: Overflow incontinence secondary to bladder outlet obstruction

correctExplanation: Urge incontinence most commonly occurs because of detrusor hyperreflexia or overactivity. It typically presents with the urge to urinate followed by the leakage of a variable amount of urine. It is most commonly associated with neurologic disorders (eg, multiple sclerosis, spinal stenosis, or spinal cord injuries) but may also be idiopathic. Physical examination and laboratory studies will show no abnormalities. Postvoid urinary bladder residual volumes will also be normal. When evaluating urinary incontinence, however, it is important to rule out an associated urinary tract infection, especially when the urinary incontinence is new in onset. Treatment of urge incontinence includes strengthening the pelvic floor, weight loss, minimizing caffeine and alcohol intake, bladder training or timed voiding, and antimuscarinic agents (eg, oxybutynin).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Detrusor hypotonia (Choice B) results in overflow incontinence caused by the inadequate contraction of the detrusor muscle to overcome the urethral sphincters, which is commonly associated with spinal cord injury and autonomic neuropathy. Overflow incontinence may also occur secondary to external sphincter hyperactivity (Choice C), which can result in bladder outlet obstruction (Choice E), along with other potential causes. Other causes of bladder outlet obstruction are benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral injury, or a urinary bladder cancer obstructing the urethral orifice. These conditions present with incontinence that manifests once there is build-up of urine within the urinary bladder lumen, which subsequently overwhelms the pressure of the urethral sphincters or obstructing lesion, resulting in the leakage of urine. External sphincter incompetence (Choice D) results in stress incontinence, which typically presents with small amounts of urine leakage associated with increases in intraabdominal pressure (eg, cough, heavy lifting). It is most common in multigravid women because of an associated weakness of the pelvic floor. It would be less likely to cause urinary urgency and frequency. Educational Objective: Urge incontinence presents with urinary urgency and leakage of variable amounts of urine caused by detrusor hyperreflexia, most commonly in the setting of neurologic disorders.

questionStem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at term has a cervix that has remained 5 cm dilated over the past 4 hours despite the administration of oxytocin . Contractions occur every 3 minutes and are 55 to 64 mm Hg by intrauterine pressure catheter measurement. Examination shows a somewhat molded vertex and considerable caput succedaneum . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Labor consists of three defined stages. The first stage is divided into latent and active labor and encompasses the start of labor (contractions and cervical change) until the completion of cervical dilation and effacement. The second stage includes the time from complete cervical dilation to the newborn's birth, and the third stage contains the delivery of the placenta. The first stage of labor is considered latent until the cervix is 4-cm dilated, after which the rate of cervical dilation increases, and the patient is in active labor. The active stage of labor can be protracted, which occurs when the cervix is dilating at less than 1 to 2 cm/hour. It can also be arrested, in which case there is no cervical change for greater than 4 hours with adequate contractions, or there is no cervical change for greater than 6 hours with inadequate contractions. Protraction and arrest can be caused by hypotonic contractions, cephalopelvic disproportion, and a non-occiput-anterior fetal presentation. Inadequate contractions occur less than three or four times in a 10-minute period with a strength of less than 200 Montevideo units (mm Hg). Both cephalopelvic disproportion and non-occiput-anterior presentation can cause molding of the fetal head and caput succedaneum, as seen in this patient. Protraction of the active phase of labor can be managed with oxytocin to augment uterine contractions and prostaglandins to assist in cervical ripening, whereas arrest of the active phase of labor is managed with cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypotonic contractions (Choice B) can cause protraction or arrest of the active stage of labor. However, this patient is having adequate uterine contractions as she is having four contractions in a 10-minute time frame with an adequate contraction strength exceeding 200 Montevideo units (mm Hg). Protracted latent phase (Choice C) of labor occurs when cervical dilation does not occur as rapidly as expected in the latent phase of labor, although the length of the latent phase is highly variable between patients. As this patient is already in active labor given her cervical dilation, this choice is incorrect. Normal active phase (Choice D) of labor is incorrect, as her cervix has not progressed in its dilation for over 4 hours despite adequate uterine contractions. This is likely because of cephalopelvic disproportion or non­ occiput-anterior presentation and will require cesarean delivery. Normal second stage (Choice E) of labor refers to the time following complete cervical dilation (10 cm) to the completed birth of the baby. As this patient is not completely dilated, she is not yet in the second stage of labor. Educational Objective: Active labor occurs from the time the cervix is 4-cm dilated until it is completely dilated at 10 centimeters. It can be protracted, when cervical dilation proceeds at a rate less than 1 to 2 cm/hour, or it can be arrested, when cervical dilation does not change in 4 hours with adequate contractions or 6 hours with inadequate contractions. Protraction is managed with oxytocin augmentation, whereas arrest necessitates cesarean delivery.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 5, para 4, at 40 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of bright red vaginal bleeding for 1 hour. Contractions have occurred every 2 to 3 minutes for 5 hours. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated . Ultrasonography at 22 weeks' gestation showed no evidence of placenta previa. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender abdomen with a firm uterus . The fetal heart rate is 140/min. On speculum examination , there is copious bright red bleeding from the external cervical os. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80% effaced . The physician informs the patient and her husband that emergency cesarean delivery is recommended . The patient and her husband state that, because of their religious beliefs, the elders of their church must agree to a surgical delivery before they can give their consent. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

choices.A: Ask the patient to convene a meeting of the church elders to discuss cesarean delivery
choices.B: Transfer the patient to another physician
choices.C: Appoint a guardian ad litem for the fetus to consent to cesarean delivery
choices.D: Obtain approval from the hospital administrator to perform emergency cesarean delivery
choices.E: Obtain approval from the pediatric staff to perform emergency cesarean delivery

correctExplanation: According to the ethical tenet of autonomy, this patient has the right to convene a meeting of the church elders to discuss cesarean delivery and potentially decline the surgery. Patients are assumed to possess decisional capacity unless they demonstrate otherwise. This patient should be assumed to have decisional capacity since she has no cognitive or psychiatric reasons to suggest the absence of capacity. Her husband's agreement supports that the patient is making a decision that is typical for her and does not reflect an absence of decisional capacity. Patients who possess decisional capacity have the ethical right to decline procedures, even if the procedures are emergent and/or involve a fetus. In patients who lack decisional capacity or are unable to communicate a decision about an emergent procedure, the ethical principle of beneficence should prevail, and the physician should save the patient's life. Having an advance directive that clearly states that the patient would not want the emergency procedure constitutes the exception to the rule of saving the incapacitated patient's life, as it can be assumed the patient possessed decisional capacity at the time the advance directive was written.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Transferring the patient to another physician (Choice B) would be inappropriate. Physicians have a duty to care for patients regardless of the physicians' agreement with patients' judgment. Appointing a guardian ad I item for the fetus to consent to cesarean delivery (Choice C) or obtaining approval from the pediatric staff to perform emergency cesarean delivery (Choice E) would violate this patient's autonomy to decide what procedures are performed on her body, which takes precedence over fetal concerns. Guardians ad litem are appointed for adult patients who are incapacitated, lack family members who could serve as surrogate decision makers, and need to consent to an urgent or emergent procedure. Obtaining approval from the hospital administrator to perform emergency cesarean delivery (Choice D) would constitute a violation of the patient's autonomy to decide about the surgery. Hospital administrators may be involved in decisions the medical team makes about incapacitated patients to navigate legal or systemic concerns. Educational Objective: Patients who possess decisional capacity have the right to decline procedures, even if the procedure is emergent and/or involves a fetus. The ethical principle of autonomy should be honored in these situations.

questionStem: A 25-year-old primigravid woman is admitted in labor at 39 weeks' gestation . The cervix is 6 cm dilated and 100% effaced . The presenting part is not palpable . Fetal heart rate is 140/min. The estimated fetal weight is 3200 g (7 lb 1 oz). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Ultrasonography of the pelvis would allow the clinician to determine the fetus' positioning when no presenting fetal part can be felt at the cervical opening. Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os. Malpresentation prevents the head from properly engaging in the pelvis for descent. For example, the excess amniotic fluid in polyhydramnios can prevent any body part from presenting at the cervical os until rupture of the membranes occurs. A serious complication that can occur in fetal malpresentation is umbilical cord prolapse. Because of the lack of occiput engagement at the cervical os, the cord can protrude through the cervix following rupture of the membranes before the baby descends into the pelvic opening. Further contractions then cause cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Given the high risk associated with vaginal deliveries in the setting of fetal malpresentation, delivery is usually completed via an elective cesarean delivery once confirmed by ultrasonography. Cord prolapse, however, is an obstetric emergency, requiring immediate cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. X-ray pelvimetry (Choice A) is a radiograph used to evaluate maternal pelvis and fetal size in the setting of suspected cephalopelvic disproportion. It may be useful in determining fetal lie but is generally not recommended when avoidable given the risk for radiation exposure to the fetus, making ultrasonography a better initial option. Oxytocin augmentation (Choice C) causes uterine contraction and is frequently used to induce labor. However, this patient is already in active labor and oxytocin augmentation would increase the risk for rupture of the membranes with cord prolapse given the potential for fetal malpresentation. Amniotomy (Choice D) refers to the manual rupture of the amniotic membrane. It is frequently used to induce labor. However, it would be dangerous to perform in this patient because of the risk for cord prolapse in the setting of fetal malpresentation. Cesarean delivery (Choice E) is generally indicated in fetal malpresentation. However, the best next step in management is to determine the fetal position with ultrasonography, rather than move directly to cesarean delivery. Prior to confirmation of the fetal lie, vaginal delivery may still be an option. Educational Objective: Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os, which prevents the head from engaging in the maternal pelvis. This increases the risk for cord prolapse with rupture of the membranes. Fetal lie can be determined by ultrasonography.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 52-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Her last visit to a physician was 4 years ago. Menses occur at regular 30- to 32-day intervals; there is no bleeding between menses . She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily but quit 5 years ago; she drinks one to two glasses of wine per week . In addition to a Pap smear, mammography, and cholesterol testing, which of the following tests is most appropriate at this time?
correctExplanation: The U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends routine screening for colorectal carcinoma in all adults between 50 to 75 years of age. Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer death in the United States. Early detection and treatment have been shown to reduce mortality. A variety of screening techniques are commonly employed, including colonoscopy performed every 10 years, test of the stool for occult blood or fecal immunochemical testing performed annually, or stool DNA testing with fecal immunochemical testing performed every 1 to 3 years. Colonoscopy carries the benefit that any visualized colonic polyps can be immediately excised and sent for histologic evaluation, making it a diagnostic and therapeutic modality.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. X-rays of the chest (Choice A) and sputum cytology (Choice C) have been used in the past to screen for lung cancer in smokers. However, these methods have poor sensitivity and specificity and are no longer recommended as screening tests for lung cancer. The preferred method for detection of lung cancer is a low-dose CT scan, which is recommended by the USPSTF in current smokers between 50 to 80 years of age with a 30 pack-year smoking history or those who have quit within the past 15 years. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice B) can be useful for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer. The USPSTF does not currently recommend routine screening for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic women. Bone densitometry (Choice D) is recommended by the USPSTF as routine screening in women over 65 years of age and in those at risk for osteoporosis. Osteoporosis risk can be assessed using standardized calculation tools such as the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool. Educational Objective: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer deaths in the United States. The mortality of colorectal cancer can be reduced by early detection and treatment. The U.S. Preventative Services Task Force currently recommends routine colorectal cancer screening in all adults between 50 and 75 years of age, which may be performed with colonoscopy or several alternative methods.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of vaginal bleeding for 2 to 5 days every 2 weeks. The flow varies from light to heavy with passage of clots. Menses previously occurred at regular 25- to 29-day intervals and lasted for 7 days with heavy flow. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . She is sexually active with one male partner, and they use condoms inconsistently . Her mother died of colon cancer, and her maternal grandmother died of breast cancer. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Her temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The uterus is normal sized. The ovaries cannot be palpated . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Test of the stool for occult blood is negative . An endometrial biopsy specimen shows grade I adenocarcinoma with atypical endometrial hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Irregular or unpredictable bleeding, or bleeding not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps) should prompt investigation for pathological causes. Endometrial carcinoma is a cause of abnormal uterine bleeding, as are cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, and endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens). Iatrogenic and idiopathic causes of abnormal uterine bleeding also occur. In women of reproductive age, pregnancy must also be ruled out as a cause of abnormal uterine bleeding. When endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma is a concern, endometrial biopsy is warranted. Risk factors for endometrial carcinoma include obesity, prolonged estrogen use, early menarche or late menopause, nulliparity, advanced age, and family history. With biopsy and imaging, the stage of endometrial carcinoma is determined and follows T (tumor), N (nodes), M (metastases) staging. If the disease is confined to the uterus, as in this patient, then surgical excision is the first line therapy. This is achieved through a hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Hormonal contraceptives include depot medroxyprogesterone {Choice A), an injectable intramuscular or subcutaneous progestin that lasts for 14 weeks and results in a sustained release of progestin, and oral contraceptives {Choice B). Oral contraceptives may be either a combination of ethinyl estradiol and progestin or progestin-only. Both methods are used to prevent pregnancy and regulate abnormal menstrual bleeding caused by anovulation or hormonal imbalances. Hormonal contraceptives are inappropriate in endometrial carcinoma, as it is often a hormonally dependent malignancy, which could result in further proliferation. Endometrial ablation {Choice C) is a potential treatment for menorrhagia in a premenopausal woman. As menorrhagia may also be caused by endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, all women undergoing endometrial ablation should have an endometrial biopsy first to exclude the presence of these conditions. Dilation and curettage {Choice D) is useful in treating heavy or abnormal uterine bleeding that does not respond to less invasive interventions, as well as for removing fetal tissue or retained products of conception. While it could debulk a portion of an endometrial tumor, it would not remove microscopic disease and would not be an appropriate treatment of endometrial carcinoma. Educational Objective: Endometrial carcinoma often presents as abnormal uterine bleeding and is diagnosed by endometrial biopsy. If the tumor has not spread distantly, surgical treatment is indicated beginning with a hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

questionStem: A 30-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 10 weeks' gestation has had fever, minimal vaginal bleeding , and severe pelvic pain for 36 hours. She says that this is an unintended pregnancy . Four months ago, she was treated with oral antibiotics for a pelvic infection . Her temperature is 40°C (104°F) . Examination shows a foul-smelling vaginal discharge and a small laceration on the cervix . The uterus is extremely tender and consistent in size with a 10-week gestation . Leukocyte count is 18,000/mm 3 with a left shift. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.B: Corpus luteum cyst I) Multiple gestation
choices.C: Ectopic pregnancy J) Pelvic inflammatory disease
choices.D: Fetal congenital abnormalities K SeP,tic abortion
choices.E: Gestational trophoblastic disease L) Single gestation
choices.G: Inevitable abortion N) Torsion of the adnexa

correctExplanation: Spontaneous abortion describes the noninduced loss of a fetus prior to 20 weeks' gestation and is subdivided into the following: threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed, and septic. In septic abortion, infection occurs within the uterine cavity. Resultant inflammation and the immune response lead to loss of the pregnancy. Symptoms of septic abortion include pelvic pain, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, vaginal bleeding, fever, and chills. Examination generally discloses uterine tenderness, cervical inflammation, and purulent cervical discharge. Treatment includes antibiotics and the evacuation of uterine contents.
incorrectExplanation: , M, and N. Acute appendicitis {Choice A) classically presents with acute, periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, along with fever, nausea, anorexia, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant. Corpus luteum cyst {Choice B), when ruptured, typically presents with acute, focal unilateral pelvic pain. If the cyst remains intact, it may be asymptomatic, or increase the risk for adnexal torsion if large. Ectopic pregnancy {Choice C) refers to fetal implantation outside of the endometrial cavity, most commonly the fallopian tube, and is often asymptomatic until large or ruptured. Rupture generally presents with acute, severe abdominopelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, and signs of peritoneal inflammation. Fetal congenital abnormalities {Choice D) may be the cause of first trimester pregnancy loss, often related to aneuploidy. Loss of a fetus with congenital abnormalities may present as a missed or complete abortion with or without a septic component. Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) {Choice E) describes trophoblast-derived tumors, which can be benign or malignant. Examples include hydatidiform moles, invasive moles, and choriocarcinoma. GTD does not typically present with fever, rather, it presents with abnormal uterine size and a 13-hCG concentration out of proportion to date of conception. Hyperemesis gravidarum {Choice F) presents as severe nausea and vomiting in association with significant weight loss (often greater than 5% of pre-pregnancy weight), ketosis or ketoacidosis, metabolic alkalosis, electrolyte abnormalities, and dehydration. It generally occurs in the first trimester. Inevitable abortion {Choice G) is characterized by the presence of an open os, typically with concomitant vaginal bleeding and cramping. Products of conception have not yet passed. Leiomyomata uteri {Choice H) are benign neoplastic tumors of the myometrial smooth muscle and are a common cause of menorrhagia. Multiple gestation {Choice I) may present with an uterine size greater than expected for gestation, morning sickness, and early pregnancy weight gain. questionStem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. She has a history of two to three seizures yearly, but she has had two seizures over the past 2 weeks . Medications include phenytoin . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Her serum phenytoin concentration is 5 µg/ml (N=10-20) . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Adding valproic acid to the medication regimen

correctExplanation: Many physiologic changes occur during pregnancy that affect drug distribution and metabolism. The physiologic increase in blood volume during pregnancy results in an increased volume of distribution for certain medications. At the same time, plasma protein concentration is decreased, resulting in more free serum medication than in the pre-pregnancy state. Additionally, the rate of hepatic metabolism and renal clearance are also typically increased. Therefore, titration of anti-epileptic drugs is commonly performed through the analysis and trending of unbound drug concentrations in the serum. While phenytoin and other anti-epileptic drugs do carry a risk for congenital malformation (eg, fetal hydantoin syndrome), teratogenicity more often occurs in the first 8 weeks of conception. Failing to provide adequate seizure control puts the mother and fetus at increased risk for pregnancy complications, including preeclampsia, stillbirth, fetal growth restriction, and prematurity. In this patient, altered pharmacodynamics have led to a decreased efficacy in her phenytoin dosage. An increase in the dosage of her current medication is the most appropriate next step to adequately prevent seizures.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Routine prenatal care (Choice A) without further adjustments to her anti-epileptic drug regimen would likely result in inadequate dosing of phenytoin, along with continued seizures, and associated pregnancy complications of prematurity, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth. Adding valproic acid to the medication regimen (Choice B) would not be the best choice for this patient, as adding a second medication exposes the mother and fetus to the risk for adverse effects without the increased likelihood of improved seizure control. Additionally, valproic acid is contraindicated in pregnancy. Switching to carbamazepine (Choice D) would be inappropriate given that the fetus has likely already been exposed to the teratogenicity of phenytoin and switching medications may not ensure adequate control of the patient's seizure activity. Carbamazepine is also associated with birth defects. Termination of the pregnancy (Choice E) is a personalized decision based on a multitude of factors. As it is unclear whether the fetus has developed any congenital abnormalities caused by its exposure to phenytoin, recommendation for pregnancy termination is inappropriate at this time. Educational Objective: The effective dosing of anti-epileptic medications (and other medications) is altered by the physiologic adaptations associated with pregnancy, such as an increased blood volume and alterations in hepatic metabolism and renal clearance. Furthermore, the teratogenic effects associated with most anti-epileptic drugs likely occur in the first eight weeks of pregnancy, while the risks associated with uncontrolled seizures persist throughout the pregnancy. Given this, it is appropriate to increase the anti-epileptic medication dose to adequately control seizures.

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of pain in her arms and numbness in her hands that awaken her from sleep. She says that her hands feel as though she had been sleeping on them. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated . Examination shows mild weakness of thumb abduction bilaterally. Sensation is decreased to pinprick in the index finger on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel of the wrist. The carpal tunnel is located anterior to the carpal bones and is bound by the flexor retinaculum. The flexor tendons of the fingers course through the tunnel, along with the median nerve. The space is rigid and does not generally permit compression, thus, any inflammatory, traumatic, or space-filling lesion may result in carpal tunnel syndrome. Patients generally present with pain and paresthesia in the median nerve dermatomal distribution, along with weakness involving the muscles of the thenar eminence. Reduced grip strength and weakness of thumb abduction may result. Symptoms are generally worse at night. Pregnancy is a known risk factor for carpal tunnel syndrome, and it is hypothesized that fluid retention expands the synovium within the tunnel, leading to nerve compression. Carpal tunnel syndrome is frequently associated with hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, ganglion cysts, obesity, acute trauma to the wrist with impingement, and chronic remodeling and scar formation following a wrist injury. Management includes treating the underlying cause, splinting of the wrist, and decompressive surgery to relieve pressure and prevent irreversible median nerve palsy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cervical radiculopathy (Choice B) presents with neuropathic pain, paresthesia, and occasionally weakness in the distribution of dermatome and myotome innervated by a particular cervical spinal root. Osteophytosis, spinal stenosis, and degenerative joint disease of the cervical spine are key risk factors. Patients generally complain of pain shooting down the arm, often in response to a triggering motion such as turning the head. Mononeuritis multiplex (Choice C) is the result of several causes such as diabetic neuropathy, vasculitis, amyloidosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus. It describes painful, asymmetric sensory and motor neuropathy involving at least two or more separate nerves. Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (Choice D) is also known as complex regional pain syndrome type 1. In general, it presents with pain and vasomotor dysfunction of an extremity, often following surgery, trauma, or an ischemic event without obvious damage to a nerve. Symptoms may be disproportionate to the expected natural history of discomfort following the inciting event. Inciting events are also often unknown. Thoracic outlet syndrome (Choice E) results from compression of the nerves and blood vessels within the thoracic outlet, and presents with pain, weakness, and atrophy of muscles in the affected extremity. While the thenar eminence is often affected, symptoms generally include the entire extremity. Educational Objective: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel of the wrist and presents with pain, paresthesia, and weakness within the distal median nerve dermatome and myotome. Pregnancy is a known risk factor for carpal tunnel syndrome, and it is hypothesized that fluid retention expands the synovium within the tunnel.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of painful episodes of menstrual cramping over the past 5 months; the pain has caused her to miss several days of school monthly. Menarche was at the age of 12 years . Her last menstrual period was 5 days ago. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of her pain?
correctExplanation: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy patients and occurs in the absence of secondary causes, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. Symptoms often begin during adolescence and commonly interfere with quality of life and with essential activities such as school or work. Patients describe cramping lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses, which persists for several days, along with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins, which stimulate painful uterine contractions. Patients are typically treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby limiting prostaglandin synthesis, or with oral hormonal contraceptives.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dermoid cyst (Choice A), also known as a mature cystic teratoma, is a common benign ovarian tumor that contains cell types from all three embryologic layers. It may present with symptoms of abdominal fullness and pain or with ovarian torsion. Dermoid cyst does not commonly present with cyclic pelvic pain. Endometriosis (Choice B) is a common cause of pelvic and abdominal pain that is caused by hormonally responsive, ectopic uterine endometrial cells. Other common features of endometriosis include dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. While endometriosis should be excluded in this patient, it is less likely than primary dysmenorrhea. Ovarian torsion (Choice C) is caused by twisting of the ovary about its ligamentous attachment with resultant compromise of its blood supply leading to ovarian ischemia. Patients present with sharp, severe, unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Psychological factors (Choice E) can contribute to the severity of dysmenorrhea, but are less likely in this patient than primary dysmenorrhea given her absence of any history suggestive of stress, depression, anxiety, or other psychological factors. Educational Objective: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy patients and occurs in the absence of secondary causes. Symptoms include crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses and persists for several days, as well as fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins that stimulate painful uterine contractions.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, at 34 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Pregnancy had been complicated by blurred vision and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight gain over the past week. Her last routine prenatal visit 1 month ago showed no abnormalities . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) , pulse is 80/min , respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 150/11 O mm Hg. Examination shows retinal arteriolar spasms and pedal edema . Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Platelet count Serum creatinine Urine protein 12.5 g/dL 8000/mm 3 200,000/mm 3 1.2 mg/dL 2+ This patient's fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following obstetric complications?
correctExplanation: This patient's findings of hypertension, proteinuria, and end-organ dysfunction occurring after the 20th week of gestation are consistent with a diagnosis of preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is caused by an abnormality of the placental spiral arteries and poor trophoblastic invasion, leading to placental hypoperfusion and the subsequent production of vasoactive hormones that cause generalized endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability, and vasospasm. It usually presents in the second or third trimester after the 20th week of gestation. Preeclampsia may lead to uteroplacental insufficiency that puts the fetus at risk for fetal growth restriction. If untreated, preeclampsia can progress to eclampsia, characterized by maternal seizures, which can have profoundly adverse outcomes including maternal stroke, cardiac arrest, renal failure, or maternal or fetal death. Preeclampsia is treated with anti-hypertensive agents, eclampsia prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate, and delivery of the fetus and placenta.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Brachia! plexus injury (Choice A) is a common obstetric complication that can occur secondary to fetal shoulder dystocia during delivery. The newborn will present with the affected arm held in adduction, with diminished grip strength and Moro reflex. Hydrops (Choice C) involves the extravasation of fluid into multiple fetal compartments and occurs secondary to multiple insults in utero, including fetal anemia or hemolysis, intrauterine or transplacental infections, congenital structural cardiac abnormalities, and chromosomal abnormalities. Preeclampsia does not increase the risk of fetal hydrops. Macrosomia (Choice D) is defined as a birth weight greater than 4000 g (8 lb 13 oz) and most commonly occurs in the setting of gestational diabetes. Preeclampsia is more frequently associated with a small fetus for gestational age. Pulmonary hypoplasia (Choice E) is commonly observed as a component of the Potter sequence and results as a sequela of oligohydramnios. Sepsis (Choice F) may result from bacterial infections secondary to preterm rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis. Preeclampsia does not significantly increase the risk of neonatal sepsis. Educational Objective: Preeclampsia is caused by abnormalities of the placental spiral arteries and poor trophoblastic invasion, leading to placental hypoperfusion and production of vasoactive hormones that cause generalized endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability, and vasospasm. It usually presents in the second or third trimester after the 20th week of gestation. Preeclampsia may lead to uteroplacental insufficiency that puts the fetus at risk for fetal growth restriction.

questionStem: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination . She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. Her diet is low in fat. She receives estrogen and progestin replacement therapy for vasomotor symptoms . Her blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following types of cancer?
correctExplanation: Exogenous estrogen raises the risk for breast and endometrial cancer; however, the concurrent use of progestin negates the effects of unopposed estrogen, drastically decreasing the risk for the development of endometrial cancer. Breast cancers can express estrogen and/or progesterone receptors, which would result in increased growth in the presence of exogenous hormone supplementation. Other risk factors for the development of breast cancer include a family history of breast cancer, genetic mutation (eg, BRCA 1 or BRCA2), early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity, and African American ethnicity. It most commonly presents with an abnormal, potentially palpable, breast lump, with or without associated skin or nipple retraction. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends a screening mammogram every 1 to 2 years for patients over 40 years of age. If a patient presents with a palpable lump, a diagnostic mammogram should be initially performed followed by an ultrasonography of the concerning region if the patient is over 30. For patients under 30, an ultrasonography or MRI should primarily be performed for evaluation, as a mammogram is typically limited by a younger patient's increased breast tissue density. If there are concerning findings for a breast malignancy, a percutaneous biopsy is warranted.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cervical (Choice B) cancer can be asymptomatic or present with postcoital bleeding. Risk factors include human papillomavirus infection with high risk strains 16, 18, 31, or 33, smoking, and immunosuppression. Estrogen is not a risk factor. Endometrial (Choice C) cancer typically presents with postmenopausal uterine bleeding, with risk factors including prolonged, unopposed exposure to estrogen, such as early menarche, late menopause, polycystic ovary syndrome, exogenous estrogen therapy, nulliparity, and obesity. The risk for endometrial cancer is decreased relative to breast cancer with the concurrent administration of progestin. Lung (Choice D) cancer commonly presents with cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, and shortness of breath. Risk factors include smoking, radon, occupational exposures, HIV infection, and radiation. Neither estrogen nor progesterone play a role in the development of lung cancer. Ovarian (Choice E) cancer typically presents indolently with abdominal distension and weight loss in a postmenopausal woman. Risk factors include a family history of ovarian cancer, genetic mutation (eg, BRCA), increased age, smoking, nulliparity, and polycystic ovary syndrome. Estrogen-progestin hormonal therapy does not play a major role in the development of ovarian cancer. Educational Objective: Hormonal therapy with progestin and estrogen significantly increases the risk for breast cancer. Other risk factors for breast cancer include a family history, genetic mutation (eg, BRCA), early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity, and African American ethnicity.

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 37 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor after an uncomplicated pregnancy . Fetal heart tones are reactive . Spontaneous rupture of membranes occurs with moderate blood-stained fluid, followed by a deep , persistent fetal heart bradycardia . The uterus is soft and nontender . The cervix is 3 cm dilated ; there is a vertex presentation . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vasa previa is a condition in which the fetal blood vessels overlie the cervical os. It is commonly associated with placenta previa, the implantation of the placenta partially or completely over the internal cervical os. Given the position of the fetal blood vessels, they are at an increased risk for rupture with the onset of labor. The rupture of membranes can result in damage to the fetal blood vessels, which causes significant fetal hemorrhage and potential fetal exsanguination and death. It classically presents with bloody amniotic fluid immediately after rupture of membranes (spontaneous or after amniotomy), with rapid onset of severe fetal distress, marked by late decelerations and persistent bradycardia. Risk factors for vasa previa include in vitro fertilization and multiple gestation pregnancies. Diagnosis is typically made prior to labor with routine screening ultrasonography, and management consists of elective cesarean delivery at 35 to 36 weeks' gestation.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Abruptio placentae (Choice A) presents with vaginal bleeding, severe uterine pain, and tetanic contractions, typically in the third trimester. It commonly results from lower abdominal trauma, smoking, or cocaine use. It is unlikely in the absence of abdominal pain and in the setting of vaginal bleeding following rupture of the membranes. Cervical cancer (Choice B) is most commonly associated with human papillomavirus high risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. It is frequently asymptomatic but can present with postcoital vaginal bleeding. It would be unlikely to cause significant vaginal bleeding with the onset of labor. Cervical polyp (Choice C) presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding, including postcoital bleeding or bleeding between menses, but would not cause significant fetal distress during labor. Ectopic pregnancy (Choice D) presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain caused by an embryo implanted outside of the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. An ectopic pregnancy is nonviable and would not survive to 37 weeks' gestation. Hydatidiform mole (Choice E) presents with nausea, vomiting, vaginal bleeding, preeclampsia, and a uterine size greater than expected. It is caused by either fertilization of an empty ovum (complete mole, no fetal parts) or dual fertilization of a normal ovum (incomplete, present fetal parts). It is nonviable and would be unlikely to be asymptomatic for 37 weeks. Incomplete abortion (Choice F) occurs when a pregnancy is lost with some expulsion of fetal tissue through an open cervical os, associated with pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks' gestation. This fetus is still alive at 37 weeks' gestation, although in distress, making an incomplete abortion incorrect. Placenta previa (Choice G) presents with painless vaginal bleeding during the third trimester caused by a placenta that partially or completely overlies the cervical os. It is a risk factor for vasa previa, but less likely to cause significant fetal hemorrhage without vasa previa. Ruptured uterus (Choice H) presents with severe abdominal pain, hemodynamic instability, uteroplacental insufficiency, sudden loss of fetal station, or fetal parts palpable above the fundus. Threatened abortion (Choice I) refers to an episode of vaginal bleeding that occurs before 20 weeks' gestation, with no loss of fetal tissue and a closed cervix. questionStem: Three months after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a newborn at term, a 24-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of pain with sexual intercourse . She breast-feeds her infant, who recently was treated for thrush. She awakens to feed him every 3 hours during the night. Her menses have not resumed . Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows an erythematous vagina with no discharge . The cervix is closed , and the uterus is normal in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Recommendation for use of a lubricant

correctExplanation: Breast-feeding women are at an increased risk for atrophic vaginitis because of the antagonistic effects of prolactin on estrogen production. In women who are not breast-feeding, atrophic vaginitis commonly occurs as a postmenopausal change. Hypoestrogenemia leads to atrophic vulvovaginal changes and can present with symptoms of irritation, itching, dryness, and dyspareunia. Examination shows atrophy of the labia, decreased secretions, and mucosal erythema and friability. Treatment includes topical estrogen and the use of lubricants during sexual intercourse. Women who also require contraception can also be treated with an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Pap smear testing (Choice B) employs a cervical swab to collect cells from the transformation zone and is an important screening tool for the detection of cervical carcinoma. Cervical carcinoma presents indolently until advanced, locally invasive, or metastatic; vaginal bleeding or post-coital spotting may be the presenting symptom. Dyspareunia is not a common symptom of cervical carcinoma. Vaginal culture (Choice C) is useful for the diagnosis and identification of antibiotic susceptibility of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative diplococcus that can cause cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, Fitz­ Hugh-Curtis syndrome, disseminated gonorrhea, septic arthritis, or urethritis. When causing vaginitis, N. gonorrhoeae typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus, although patients may be asymptomatic. Antibiotic therapy (Choice D) is useful for the treatment of sexually transmitted infections, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. These infections commonly cause cervicitis and present with abnormal discharge. Antifungal therapy (Choice E) is useful for treating vulvovaginitis secondary to Candida albicans. Candida! vulvovaginitis presents with signs and symptoms of vaginal pruritus, vu Ivar erythema, and thick, white discharge. This diagnosis is less likely given the patient's history of breastfeeding and absence of risk factors for candidal vulvovaginitis, such as the use of antibiotics, oral contraceptives, intravaginal or intrauterine contraceptive devices, or history of immunocompromise. Educational Objective: Breast-feeding women are at an increased risk for atrophic vaginitis because of the antagonistic effects of prolactin on estrogen production. Treatment includes topical estrogen and the use of lubricants during sexual intercourse.

questionStem: A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 41 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Contractions occur every 3 minutes. The cervix is 100% effaced and 4 cm dilated; the vertex is at +1 station . The membranes rupture yielding moderately thick meconium-stained fluid. The fetal heart rate has a baseline of 130/min with variable decelerations lasting 45 seconds and decreasing to 60/min . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Variable decelerations following the rupture of membranes are suggestive of umbilical cord compression. Amnioinfusion is the process of instilling fluid into the amniotic cavity. Amnioinfusion is useful for alleviating umbilical cord compression by increasing the volume of fluid in the amniotic cavity. Although amnioinfusion is the most correct response of the options provided here, evidence for the benefit of amnioinfusion towards improving outcomes related to meconium-stained amniotic fluid remains controversial.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. External cephalic version (Choice A) is a technique for repositioning the fetus when breech presentation is detected and may be performed after 37 weeks' gestation. External cephalic version is not routinely used for the management of umbilical cord compression and carries a risk of worsening compression or entanglement of the umbilical cord. Forceps delivery (Choice B) is useful for assisting vaginal delivery. If fetal distress is detected because of persistent umbilical cord compression, emergency cesarean delivery is the preferred method of delivery, rather than forceps delivery. Amniocentesis (Choice D) involves the ultrasonography-guided needle aspiration of fluid from the amniotic cavity. It is useful for the diagnosis of fetal chromosomal abnormalities and of chorioamnionitis. Removal of further amniotic fluid in the setting of cord compression is likely to worsen compression and fetal hypoxia and should not be performed. Cordocentesis (Choice E) involves the ultrasonography-guided needle aspiration of blood from the fetal umbilical cord. Sampling of fetal blood from the umbilical cord carries risk and should only be used when less invasive techniques provide inadequate or inconclusive information. It is not appropriate in the diagnosis or management of umbilical cord compression. Educational Objective: Variable decelerations following the rupture of membranes is suggestive of umbilical cord compression. Amnioinfusion is the process of instilling fluid into the amniotic cavity. Amnioinfusion is useful for alleviating fetal cord compression by increasing the volume of fluid in the amniotic cavity.

questionStem: A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has had increasingly severe dysmenorrhea over the past 2 years and dyspareunia and pain with defecation for 6 months . She has been unable to conceive for 2 years . Pelvic examination shows a fixed , tender , retroverted uterus , nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments , and tender adnexa bilaterally ; there is a 5-cm , tender , cystic , right adnexal mass . A pregnancy test is negative .

choices.F: Endometriosis N) Ruptured corpus luteum cyst

correctExplanation: Endometriosis, the presence of ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, may occur close to the uterus, such as on the cervix, within a fallopian tube, on the broad ligament, or on an ovary. The tissue may also be distant, such as on the visceral peritoneal surface of the intestines or rectum, within the peritoneal cavity, or within the thorax. Endometrial tissue remains hormonally sensitive, and symptoms often fluctuate on a cyclic, monthly basis as the tissue progresses through the histologic phases of proliferative and secretory endometrium, then sloughs during menses. Symptoms include chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. Physical examination may include tenderness to palpation of the affected structures or visualization of an endometrial implant on the cervix or vaginal wall. Diagnosis of endometriosis is definitively made through laparoscopy to visualize and sample endometriotic implants.

questionStem: A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-week history of bloody nipple discharge from the left breast. Examination of the breasts shows no palpable masses or skin retraction . Blood can be expressed from a ductal element of the nipple of the left breast. Mammography shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: lntraductal papilloma is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge, which may reflect malignant pathology if present in the setting of a palpable breast mass. lntraductal papillomas are benign tumors originating from the walls of lactiferous ducts and proliferate into the ductal lumen. The papilloma is usually too small to be palpated externally. lntraductal papillomas can be solitary or multiple. Initial diagnosis is typically made by ultrasonography and core needle biopsy. A small portion of intraductal papillomas contain regions of atypical cells or ductal carcinoma in situ. Removal of the papilloma can be performed with surgical excision or microdochectomy (excision of a lactiferous duct), which facilitates more detailed histopathologic analysis.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Fat necrosis (Choice A) is often detected in the breast as a palpable nodularity in an area of previous trauma. On imaging, peripheral calcifications are often seen. Fibroadenoma (Choice B) presents as a unilateral, nontender, mobile, rubbery mass in the breast, often in a younger woman. They are typically benign. Fibrocystic changes of the breast (Choice C) present with various sites of breast pain and lumps, which may be bilateral. The lesions may respond to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle. Fibrocystic changes are benign. Galactorrhea (Choice D) is the spontaneous discharge of milk from a breast that occurs outside of normal postpartum lactation. While often benign, galactorrhea may indicate hyperprolactinemia secondary to a pituitary adenoma. Infiltrating ductal carcinoma (Choice E) is the most common form of breast carcinoma and often presents as a painless lump, although many patients are asymptomatic. Mammography may show microcalcifications and/or an infiltrative mass. Diagnosis is made by core needle biopsy or excisional biopsy. Mastitis (Choice G) presents with erythema and induration of the breast in an area of tender, warm skin. It classically occurs in breastfeeding mothers as a consequence of nipple trauma leading to inoculation from cutaneous or oral flora. Paget disease of the breast (Choice H) presents with eczema-like patches on the nipple. It is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma of the breast. questionStem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks' gestation has had ruptured membranes for 5 hours without contractions . Her prenatal course was uncomplicated . Her cervix is 80% effaced and 2 cm dilated. The fetal position is right occipitoposterior . The fetal heart rate pattern is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern?
correctExplanation: Minimal variability, which is defined as less than six beats per minute variation from the baseline heart rate, as seen in this case, can be caused by the fetal sleep state, hypoxia, opioids, and magnesium. When caused by hypoxia, the fetal heart tracing will also typically show either tachycardia or bradycardia (depending on the severity of hypoxia) along with late or variable decelerations. This can indicate uteroplacental insufficiency or umbilical cord compression, respectively. As this patient shows no sign of distress, the fetal heart rate is normal, and there has been no administration of opioids or magnesium, the minimal variability seen in this tracing is most likely caused by a fetal sleep state.

Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation. questionStem: A 42-year-old woman , gravida 5, para 5, comes to the physician requesting advice regarding contraception . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals . Her last menstrual period was 3 days ago. She has hypertension treated with a 13-adrenergic blocking agent , but she often forgets to take it. At the age of 21 years , she was treated for Chlamydia trachomatis infection. During her second pregnancy , a Pap smear was reported as a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; after delivery, a follow-up Pap smear showed no abnormalities . Since that time, she has had no abnormal Pap smears . She is sexually active and monogamous with her husband . Physical examination , including pelvic examination , shows no abnormalities. She desires the most effective contraception that she will easily remember to use. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding contraception for this patient?
correctExplanation: An intrauterine device (IUD) is a long-acting reversible contraceptive option that does not require active compliance on the part of the patient. Both copper and levonorgestrel IUDs are available. The copper IUD provides a contraceptive method without the use of hormones. Copper is spermicidal and inhibits sperm motility and the acrosomal reaction necessary for fertilization. As well, it induces local inflammatory changes of the endometrium and increases cervical mucus production, further decreasing the chance of successful sperm passage or embryonic implantation in the endometrium. Potential complications include increased menstrual flow and pain during menses. Hormonal IUDs also cause cervical mucous thickening and induce glandular atrophy of the endometrium, preventing implantation. IUDs are a reliable form of contraception with failure rates as low as 1 %. Depending on the type, they may be kept in place for up to ten years.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Condoms (Choice A) come in both male and female varieties. Both must be placed prior to intercourse to be effective. While they are less effective than hormonal or IUD forms of contraception and have high failure rates, they do provide protection from sexually transmitted infections. Oral contraceptives (Choice B), which are taken daily, and depot medroxyprogesterone (Choice D), which is injected every 14 weeks (approximately 3 months), are both forms of hormonal contraception. Neither would be optimal in a patient with concerns for medication compliance. Additionally, though not applicable in this case, hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in patients with a history of thromboembolic disorders, liver dysfunction, and breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. A diaphragm (Choice C) is a barrier contraceptive that fits on top of the cervix and anterior wall of the vagina. It must be placed prior to intercourse and left in for 6 to 8 hours after use. It is typically used with spermicide. Diaphragms are not as effective at preventing pregnancy compared to an IUD. Educational Objective: IUDs are one of the most reliable forms of contraception because they do not depend on patient compliance. Failure rates of IUDs are low.

questionStem: Two days after a cesarean delivery for fetal distress , a 27-year-old woman has temperatures to 38.2°C (100 .8°F) . She had an 8-hour labor complicated by mild meconium-stained amniotic fluid . Membranes ruptured 2 hours after admission . Breath sounds are decreased at both lung bases . Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness below the umbilicus and a well-healing incision . There is a moderate amount of lochia with no odor. Examination of the lower extremities shows edema and no tenderness . Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.8 g/dl , leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3, and platelet count is 189,000/mm 3. A urine catheter specimen is negative . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A Atelectasis G) Pulmonary embolism
correctExplanation: Atelectasis refers to the partial or complete collapse or incomplete expansion of pulmonary parenchyma. There are multiple types of atelectasis, including obstructive, passive, compressive, cicatricial, and adhesive. It is most common in patients who are gravid, immobile, or in the postsurgical state, who are unable to produce adequate tidal volume to expand the lungs. In gravid patients or patients who have just undergone vaginal delivery, increased intra-abdominal pressure, caused by the gravid uterus, pushes on the diaphragm and intrathoracic cavity thus decreasing the ability of the lungs to expand normally. Physical examination will show diminished respiratory effort, often with reduced breath sounds at the lung bases corresponding to the regions of non-aerated, collapsed lung and inadequate diaphragmatic excursion. Pain control, incentive spirometry, and respiratory therapy with lung expansion maneuvers are key initial steps in management.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Deep venous thrombosis (Choice B) formation is promoted with venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. It would typically present with unilateral extremity edema. Endometritis (Choice C) is an acute, typically polymicrobial, infection of the uterine endometrium. Patients typically present with fever, tenderness of the uterine fundus, and mucopurulent vaginal discharge. A risk factor for the development of endometritis includes prolonged rupture of membranes (greater than 18 hours) and would be unlikely in this patient. Episiotomy infection (Choice D) would present with induration, erythema, and purulent drainage from an episiotomy incision placed during delivery. It would be unlikely in this patient with a well-healing incision. Mastitis (Choice E) presents with erythema and induration in an area of tender, warm skin of the breast. It classically occurs in breastfeeding mothers as a consequence of nipple trauma leading to inoculation from cutaneous or oral flora. It would be unlikely in this patient just after delivery. Pneumonia (Choice F) is characterized by fever, a cough productive of sputum, malaise, and chest discomfort. On physical examination, there may be abnormal lung sounds such as rales or rhonchi, along with increased tactile fremitus. Pulmonary embolism (Choice G) is characteristically associated with long periods of immobilization and deep venous thrombosis formation from venous stasis. Classic symptoms include pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea; if a pulmonary infarction occurs, hemoptysis may be present. Vital signs are often notable for tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Pyelonephritis (Choice H) and urinary tract infection (Choice K) would present with pyuria, leukocyte esterase, and nitrites. Lower urinary tract infections would present with dysuria, urinary urgency, and frequency, and pyelonephritis may present with flank pain, nausea, and vomiting. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (Choice I) is a rare sequela of endometritis that can lead to local invasion and infection of the pelvic vein walls, which causes intimal damage and thrombosis. This condition typically presents with pelvic pain and fever, which is often widely variable in course, ranging from normal temperature to extremely high. Diagnosis typically occurs through blood cultures.
